subject: science
title: Understand materials and their properties
promise: This starts from the difference between a THING and what it is MADE OF — and once you can see that, choosing the right material for a job, and testing materials fairly, both make sense.

sections.heading: An object and its material are different things
sections.body:
A spoon is an OBJECT — a thing with a job. What the spoon is MADE OF is its MATERIAL: metal, plastic, or wood.
The same object can be made from different materials (a metal spoon, a wooden spoon), and the same material can make different objects (a metal spoon, a metal gate, a metal coin).
When scientists talk about materials, they mean the stuff itself — and every question in this topic starts by separating the thing from the stuff.
sections.example: A window is an object. Glass is the material it is made from — and glass also makes bottles, lenses and jars.

sections.heading: Properties: what a material is like
sections.body:
A PROPERTY is something a material is like, wherever you find it. Glass is transparent — you can see through it. Metal is hard and strong. Wool is soft and warm. Rubber is flexible — it bends without breaking — and elastic, springing back afterwards.
Some useful property words: hard or soft, rough or smooth, transparent or opaque, waterproof or absorbent, magnetic or not, bendy or rigid.
Properties belong to the MATERIAL, not the object: every glass window is transparent, because that is what glass is like.
sections.example: A sponge is absorbent — it soaks up water. A raincoat is waterproof — water runs off it.

sections.heading: Solids, liquids and gases
sections.body:
Every material is in one of three STATES.
A SOLID keeps its own shape — a stone stays stone-shaped wherever you put it.
A LIQUID flows, and takes the shape of whatever container holds it — pour water from a cup into a bowl and it becomes bowl-shaped — but its amount stays the same.
A GAS spreads out to fill all the space it can. The air around you is a gas; it fills the whole room, corners included.
Solids you can hold; liquids you can pour; gases usually you cannot even see.
sections.example: Water in a bottle is bottle-shaped. Tip it into a glass and the same water is glass-shaped — liquids take their container's shape.

sections.heading: Choosing the right material for the job
sections.body:
Materials are chosen FOR their properties. A window must let light through, so it is made of transparent glass. A saucepan must not melt or burn on the cooker, so it is metal. Wellington boots must keep water out, so they are waterproof rubber.
Run the logic both ways: from the job, ask what properties are needed; from the material, ask what jobs it suits. A chocolate teapot fails because chocolate's properties — it melts when warm — are exactly wrong for holding hot tea.
sections.example: A firefighter's jacket needs to resist heat and keep water out — so it is made from special heat-resistant, waterproof fabric, not wool.

sections.heading: Testing materials fairly
sections.body:
How would you find out which paper towel is most absorbent? TEST them — but test them FAIRLY.
A fair test changes only ONE thing (the towel) and keeps everything else the same: the same amount of water, the same size of towel, the same soaking time. If one towel got more water or more time, the test could not tell you which towel was better — only which test was easier.
Scientists call the things you keep the same the CONTROLLED things. One change, everything else equal — that is what makes a result trustworthy.
sections.example: Testing which cup keeps tea warm longest: same amount of tea, same starting temperature, same room — only the cup changes.

mistakes.right: The spoon is the OBJECT; its material is metal, wood or plastic — the stuff it is made from.
mistakes.why: Objects have jobs; materials have properties. Science questions are almost always about the material.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking a liquid changes amount when it is poured into a taller, thinner glass.
mistakes.right: The liquid changes SHAPE to match its container — the amount stays exactly the same.
mistakes.why: Looking taller is not being more. Pour it back and it fills the first container just as before.

mistakes.wrong: Testing two paper towels with different amounts of water and picking a winner.
mistakes.right: Change only the towel; keep the water, size and time the same for both.
mistakes.why: If two things changed, you cannot tell which one caused the result — the test is unfair and its answer means nothing.

check.question: A window is made of glass. Which is the MATERIAL?
check.explanation: The window is the object; glass is the stuff it is made from. Transparent is a property of glass.

check.question: What does TRANSPARENT mean?
check.explanation: Transparent materials, like glass, let light pass through so you can see through them.

check.question: Which state of matter keeps its own shape?
check.explanation: Solids keep their shape; liquids take their container's shape; gases spread out to fill the space.

check.question: What does a liquid do when you pour it from a cup into a bowl?
options: It takes the shape of the bowl
check.answer: It takes the shape of the bowl
check.explanation: Liquids flow and take their container's shape — but the amount stays the same.

check.question: Which state of matter spreads out to fill all the space it can?
check.explanation: Gases, like the air in a room, spread to fill every corner of their container.

check.question: Why are saucepans made of metal rather than chocolate?
options: Metal does not melt at cooking heat
check.answer: Metal does not melt at cooking heat
check.explanation: A material is chosen for its properties — a saucepan must survive the cooker's heat, and chocolate melts.

check.question: What does ABSORBENT mean?
check.explanation: Absorbent materials, like sponges and paper towels, soak liquid up. Waterproof is the opposite idea.

check.question: In a fair test of which paper towel is most absorbent, what should CHANGE?
options: The towel and the amount of water
check.explanation: A fair test changes one thing and keeps all the rest the same — otherwise you cannot tell what caused the result.

check.question: Which property should wellington boots have?
check.explanation: Boots for puddles must keep water OUT — waterproof, the opposite of absorbent.

check.question: Which of these is a PROPERTY of a material?
check.explanation: Properties describe what the material itself is like — flexible, hard, transparent — wherever it is and whatever it makes.

practice.prompt: Name the OBJECT and the MATERIAL: a wooden chair.
practice.answer: The chair is the object; wood is the material.
practice.hint: The thing with a job, and the stuff it is made from.

practice.prompt: Which state of matter is the air in a balloon?
practice.hint: It spreads out to fill the whole balloon.

practice.prompt: Give one property a raincoat's material must have.
practice.hint: What must happen when rain lands on it?

practice.prompt: What shape does milk take when you pour it into a glass?
practice.hint: It is a liquid — what do liquids do in a container?

practice.prompt: Give two properties of glass that make it right for windows.
practice.answer: It is transparent (lets light through) and hard/rigid (keeps its shape and protects).
practice.hint: Why can you see the garden, and why does the wind not bend it?

practice.prompt: Name one material that IS magnetic and one that is NOT.
practice.answer: Iron (or steel) is magnetic; plastic (or wood, glass) is not.
practice.hint: Which materials does a fridge magnet stick to?

practice.prompt: A towel and a plastic bag are left in the rain. Which one soaks up water, and what is that property called?
practice.answer: The towel soaks up water — it is absorbent. The plastic bag is waterproof.
practice.hint: One material drinks the water; one turns it away.

practice.prompt: Explain why a solid keeps its shape but a liquid does not.
practice.answer: A solid holds itself together in a fixed shape; a liquid flows, so it spreads to fit whatever container holds it.
practice.hint: Think of a stone and some water, each put into a bowl.

practice.prompt: You test which of three cups keeps tea warm longest. Name TWO things that must stay the same.
practice.answer: The amount of tea and its starting temperature (also: the room, the time you wait).

practice.prompt: Why would a metal handle on a cooking pot be a poor choice, even though metal suits the pot itself?
practice.answer: Metal lets heat travel through it, so the handle would get too hot to hold — handles are made of wood or plastic, which stay cooler.
practice.hint: What does metal do with heat that wood does not?

practice.prompt: A test compares two papers' strength, but one strip is wider than the other. Why is the result worthless?
practice.answer: Two things changed at once (the paper AND the width), so you cannot tell whether the winner was stronger paper or just a wider strip.
practice.hint: How many things is a fair test allowed to change?

practice.prompt: Give an example of the same material making two very different objects, and the property that suits both.
practice.answer: Glass makes windows and bottles — it is transparent and waterproof, which suits letting light in and holding liquid. (Other good answers exist.)
practice.hint: Pick a material, then think of two jobs its properties fit.
